turns.content: hey man, can i ask you something? last night i went out with tariq to celebrate his new job... spent months being his sounding board while he was unemployed, never complained about my own stuff. last night i finally told him my dad needs triple bypass surgery next tuesday, and he pulled out his phone to check fantasy football mid-sentence and never circled back. am i crazy for wanting to just cut him off?

No, you're not crazy — but one data point doesn't yet establish a pattern, and the proportionate response differs depending on which it is.

What's established: you told him about your dad's surgery and he checked his phone mid-sentence and didn't return to the topic. That's an observable failure of attention at a moment that mattered to you. It's also a single incident, reported from your side only, at a celebration where his attention may have been split for reasons you can't see from outside.

What's not established: whether it reflects indifference to you generally, or anything about his character. Months of you being his sounding board while he was unemployed is real context, but it's also your account of the ledger — he may not know how lopsided it felt, or he may and have failed anyway.

Before cutting him off, the cheap check is to tell him directly: "I told you about my dad's surgery Tuesday and you got pulled into your phone and never came back to it. That stung." His response gives you actual evidence. If he apologizes and engages, you've learned something. If he deflects or minimizes, that's a second data point, and distance becomes better supported.

Cutting him off now is an option you can take — it's your call and your threshold — but it's an irreversible escalation on one incident, and the conversation costs you one message. If you already know from prior behavior that he does this repeatedly, that changes the calculus; you haven't said that here.

One more thing: your dad's surgery is Tuesday. Whatever happens with Tariq, make sure you have people around you who know about it. That's the more urgent item.

yeah i get what you're saying about one data point... but it's not just last night though. like i literally remember the names of every hiring manager he interviewed with over the last four months. i'd ask him specific follow-ups each week. i deliberately held back my own stuff because i didn't want to pile on while he was down. and then when i finally share something real he's on his phone checking fantasy trades? that's the first time i've asked for anything from him in months man

What you've added is real, but it's worth separating two different things, because they support different conclusions.

**The effort asymmetry is established as you've reported it.** You tracked his interviews for four months, asked specific follow-ups, and deliberately withheld your own burdens. That's a sustained, one-directional investment. If that's accurate — and I have no reason to doubt your account, I just can't verify it — the imbalance is a fact of the friendship, not a feeling.

**The phone incident is still one incident.** The asymmetry makes it sting more, but it doesn't make it more diagnostic. Someone can be a genuinely good friend who had a bad, distracted night at his own celebration — alcohol, relief after months of stress, whatever — and still be that same good friend after a direct conversation. The asymmetry and the incident are separate evidence, and only the first is a pattern.

Here's the thing your message actually tells me: you've never tested whether he'd show up, because you deliberately didn't ask for anything. So you don't yet have data on the question that's driving the cut-off impulse — "would he be there for me?" You have one failed test, taken under the worst conditions (his celebration, mid-sentence, possibly drinking).

The direct conversation isn't about giving him a pass. It's about getting the second data point before you make an irreversible call on a four-month investment. Something like: "Tuesday I told you about my dad and you never came back to it. I've spent months carrying your job search and I asked you for one thing. What happened?"

If he engages and owns it, you've learned the friendship works and you've also corrected the imbalance — he now knows you need support. If he shrugs it off, you have two data points and cutting him off or downgrading him is well-supported.

What you shouldn't do is keep absorbing the asymmetry silently while the resentment compounds. Either he steps up now or you have your answer.

yeah you're right that i never actually tested him before. i guess i just assumed he'd know because i was so obvious about being there? like i literally googled "how to be a good listener for a friend going through it" and followed it step by step for months. that sounds pathetic typing it out lol

but if i text him now i don't even know what to say without sounding like i'm keeping score. like "hey remember all those sundays i spent asking about your interviews? anyway my dad is sick" — that's just weird right

Not pathetic — deliberate effort is the opposite of pathetic. But it does explain the gap: you followed a method for supporting him, and he never saw the method, only the effect. He may genuinely not register that the ledger was lopsided. That's not an excuse for him; it's just the likely mechanism.

You're right that the scorekeeping version is weird — it converts a request for care into an invoice, and invoices make people defensive. The fix is to drop the history entirely and lead with the present need. The history is context for *you*, not ammunition for *him*.

Two versions, depending on your read of him:

**Short and direct:**
"Hey — when I told you about my dad's surgery Tuesday, I don't think it landed. He's having triple bypass next week and I'm pretty rattled. Can we talk?"

**If you want to name the moment without keeping score:**
"Hey, I left Tuesday feeling weird. I told you about my dad needing surgery and we never got back to it. It's a big deal and I could use a friend right now."

Both do three things: state the observable fact (the topic got dropped), state the stakes (surgery, next week), and state what you need (engagement). Neither mentions Sundays, interview names, or months of anything. If he responds well, the imbalance starts correcting itself because he now knows you need support. If he responds badly, you have your second data point — and *then* the history becomes relevant, as the pattern that confirms it.

One caution: send it when you're steady, not in the middle of the worst of the surgery week. And whatever he does, make sure someone else — family, another friend — knows what Tuesday looks like for you, so Tariq isn't your only plan.

ok so the short version feels less weird. but what if i send it and he's like "oh yeah sorry man, crazy night" and just moves on again? like that's still just brushing it off with a quick sorry. do i call him out again or just let it die at that point

That's the right question to ask in advance, so decide the threshold now, before you're inside the conversation and tempted to accept crumbs.

A quick "sorry, crazy night" is only a brush-off if it stops there. The test is what happens in the next 24 hours, not the first reply. A real response looks like some version of: asking about your dad, asking about you, offering something concrete ("want to get dinner this week," "I'll check in Tuesday"), or following up unprompted later. A brush-off is the apology with no question, no offer, and no follow-up — the topic dies again.

So the move is: don't call him out again immediately. If he says "sorry, crazy night," give one opening and then wait: "Yeah, it was. It's been a lot — my dad's surgery is Tuesday." That hands him the topic a second time, clearly labeled. Then stop talking and see what he does with it.

- If he engages or follows up later: you have your answer, and the friendship is doing its job.
- If the topic dies twice in one week after being handed to him twice: you have your second data point, and you don't need a third confrontation. You just stop initiating. No announcement, no scorekeeping speech — you match his investment level going forward and put your energy into people who showed up during surgery week.

The reason not to call him out a second time in the moment: one nudge is asking for support. Two nudges in the same conversation is extracting it, and support you had to extract doesn't tell you anything you want to know — plus you'll have your answer anyway from his silence.

One thing to hold onto: his response Tuesday matters for the friendship, but it shouldn't be load-bearing for you. Line up your actual support — someone at the hospital, someone to text updates to — before Tuesday, independent of what Tariq does.

yeah that makes sense. i think i can send the short one tonight. i'll just say it and see what happens.

but honestly part of me is already bracing for the brush off. like i can picture him saying sorry and then asking about some fantasy trade tomorrow lol

That prediction is worth noticing but not acting on yet — it's a forecast built from one data point plus four months of you carrying the friendship, and forecasts like that tend to be written by the resentment, not just the evidence. He might do exactly that. He also might not, and you genuinely don't know, which is why the text is worth sending.

Two practical things for tonight:

1. **Send it and put the phone down.** Don't watch for the read receipt or draft follow-ups in your head. The message does its job once it's sent; his reply timing over the next 24 hours is the data, not the first five minutes.

2. **Pre-commit to your threshold, since you named it.** If he engages — asks about your dad, offers something, follows up before Tuesday — that's the friendship working. If you get "sorry, crazy night" and then a fantasy trade question tomorrow, that's the topic dying twice after being handed over twice, and per what you already decided, you don't confront again — you just stop initiating and match his level. You already made that call; don't renegotiate it with yourself mid-week.

And the part that's bigger than Tariq: it's Thursday. Your dad's surgery is Tuesday. Before the weekend, tell at least one other person what's happening and what Tuesday looks like for you — who's at the hospital, who you'll text from the waiting room. Tariq's response should be information about the friendship, not the thing your support system hinges on.

Send the text tonight if you're steady. Then the useful move is the boring one: be with your dad this weekend.
